newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - Pension woes at South Africa's parastatals.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Pension woes at South Africa's parastatals.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd
Ten years ago, in his "En Route to Fairyland", Dr Wassenaar wrote of the impending disaster of the state pension funds.

What he had to say of state pension funds applied fully to the parastatal pension funds that were equally defined benefit funds that were committed to benefits, impossibly - actuarially speaking - beyond the capacity of the funds to honour.

It was not simply a matter of their restricted portfolio allocations in that the investment of the funds were confined to public sector bonds. Quite clearly there has been a prolonged period of either wilful or, to be charitable, naively innocent swelling of benefits, ultimately in relation to final salaries augmented by buy-back arrangements, with even low-interest loans being made available for the purpose.
Successive Ministers of Finance failed in their responsibilities to ensure the actuarial viability of the funds and, indeed, actuaries were dispensed with.

The worm has begun to turn. A situation has now arisen in the case of Transnet with its entire operating surplus being devoted to the servicing of the 19 million rand stock that was issued to the Transnet Pension Fund to cover the deficit. There has been general upset that there is nothing left for either upgrading or maintaining its infrastructure. In effect, the organisation exists for the benefit of its pension fund.

The Stride Committee looking into the matter has recommended that Transnet's pension responsibilities be transferred to the State, in order to make the parastatal profitable. Heaven forbid! The transfer would help Transnet but would totally upset the State's finances.

The present fiscal plight of the State lies in the fact that it carries an excessive debt burden of the order of 55 percent of GDP, which has to be serviced at an average coupon rate of nearly 11.25 percent resulting in a specific interest bill of 6.2 percent of GDP. This compares with the Maastricht parameters of 60 percent debt at an average coupon rate of less than five percent, giving an interest bill of less than three percent of GDP. Our predicament lies in the regime of high interest rates that has prevailed for many years.

With government's longer-term fiscal objective being the attainment of a three percent budgetary deficit, as set out in the GEAR document, there has to be a continuous deflationary primary surplus of revenue over non-interest expenditure as well as the application of whatever privatisation poceeds and other capital revenues that arise to the reduction of the debt. This is apparent from the mathematical identity of the budget deficit ratio being equal to the interest bill ratio less the primary surplus ratio and other capital contributions. Thus the extent of the public debt compels a deflationary fiscal stance.

The state pension funds are in serious deficit and it is understood that there is a long term plan through to year 2010 to bring about actuarial balance. Besides a degree of privatisation of the investment of the funds and a diversification into equities, which do not impact on the state finances, there are two measures which do.

These are the extraordinarily high ratio of employer to employee contribution of 2.74 compared with 1.5 as the norm and exceptionally 2.0 in the private sector and specific capital transfers involving the public debt. These have amounted to 12.1 billion rand, comprising 5.2 billion from the proceeds of market issues and 6.9 billion rand direct notes to the pension funds at an average coupon rate of 13.5 percent. Despite these measures the shortfall in the funds amounted to 54.4 billion rand in March 1996, the equivalent of nearly 20 percent of the total public debt. As a contingent liability the shortfall is not included in the public debt.

The actuarial balance to the state pension funds could be established overnight by covering the deficit with an interest-bearing note, but this would add more than seven billion rand to the State's interest bill and raise this year's deficit from four percent of GDP to 5.2 percent. Thus efforts to improve the balance of the funds run counter to the objectives of fiscal rectitude.

There is an unholy impasse represented by the conflicting aims of full financial viability of the funds and reducing fiscal deficits. There are possible resolutions to the problem which may be forced on government eventually. These have to be explored and they lie in the alternatives of pay-as-you-go schemes that were forced on governments elsewhere in the world, radically revising the pension benefits or freezing them and floating off the problem through inflation, or going over to defined contribution schemes in place of the defined benefits.

But certainly, the problems of the State Pension Funds should not be compounded by the absorption of Transnet's pension liabilities. The Stride Committee will have to think again. The 19 billion rand stock will have to be cancelled and a longer term solution fashioned.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
